newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram says 8 pct GDP growth possible.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram says 8 pct GDP growth possible.

text.p: Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram said India was capable of raising its annual economic growth rate to eight percent by the end of the century but needed to remove remaining controls over business to eradicate poverty.
"There is no doubt that we can easily sustain seven percent growth and by the turn of the century we can achieve eight percent growth," Chidambaram told a meeting of business leaders in the capital.

In the 1996/97 fiscal year that ended on March 31, India's gross domestic product grew by 6.8 percent. Over the past three fiscal years, average annual GDP growth has been seven percent, up from about 3.5 percent between 1950 and 1980, and 5.5 percent in the 1980s, he said.

The finance minister said that despite the strengthening of India's growth since free-market economic reforms were launched in 1991, some continued to hold the belief that a more robust economy, particularly industry, will not alleviate poverty.
"In the past year and a half, the debate about liberalisation has acquired a very sharp edge," he said.
Chidambaram cited "very sharp differences" within Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's 15-party centre-left coalition which ranges from free traders like himself to communists.
"A lot of well-meaning people genuinely believe that growth, particularly growth led by industry, will not abolish poverty in this country," he said.
"I don't share this diagnosis. Unless we meet this argument, it will be difficult to move forward."
Citing Thailand and Malaysia, Chidambaram said other countries had abolished poverty in far fewer than the 50-year period during which India has been independent.
Chidambaram called on industry to help convince the nation liberalisation will spur growth and wipe out poverty by 2020.
"We can do that only by accelerating growth," he said, adding that China had proved that a country can maintain a double-digit economic growth rate with low inflation.
"The higher growth, the higher capacity the government has to appropriate money to make a frontal attack on poverty."

The finance minister said the government needed to press ahead with removing controls over agriculture, services including insurance, and industry. "We need to deregulate sectors that are highly regulated," he said.

"I am confident that we will inject a measure of competition into the services sector, including insurance," he said, noting that the government recently failed to muster enough support in parliament to defeat a measure that would bar foreign insurers.
Chidambaram said sectors which continued to be highly regulated -- coal, power, petroleum, roads -- performed poorly in 1996/97. "We must continue de-monopolisation for higher productivity," he said.
The finance minister said poverty could be eradicated if the economy grew at an average of eight percent a year.

"At the end of the next 20 years, if we continue to grow at seven to eight percent, we would not only have made India the fourth largest economy in the world, we would have also abolished poverty as we have known it for 5,000 years."
